title: Association between long-term (current) aspirin use and sepsis-related delirium in elderly patients: a retrospective cohort study

sections.abstract:
Driven by the global aging trend, the prognosis of elderly patients with sepsis has garnered increasing attention. Sepsis-associated delirium (SAD), a common manifestation of elderly patients with sepsis, is frequently linked to poor clinical outcomes. Despite its prevalence, effective preventive measures remain lacking. Pharmacological interventions have emerged as promising components of a comprehensive strategy for the treatment and prevention of delirium. Among them, aspirin—renowned for its anti-inflammatory properties, affordability, and safety—may hold particular promise, given the central role of inflammation in the pathogenesis of both sepsis and delirium. Early initiation of anti-inflammatory therapy may offer a more effective approach to preventing SAD and enhancing patient outcomes.

To investigate the association between long-term (current) aspirin use and the incidence of SAD in elderly septic patients.

We extracted and analyzed data from 9145 elderly septic patients. The primary outcome, SAD, was analyzed using multivariable logistic regression to explore the correlation between long-term (current) aspirin use and the incidence of SAD. To ensure the robustness of the results, inverse probability of treatment weighting was used to adjust Intergroup relations. Finally, subgroup analyses were conducted.

765 elderly septic patients were long-term (current) aspirin users, with a SAD incidence rate of 31.9% (244/765). In contrast, 8380 elderly septic patients without a history of long-term (current) aspirin use had a SAD incidence rate of 46.1% (3863/8380). After adjusting for 49 covariates, the multivariable logistic regression results showed that long-term (current) aspirin use was negatively associated with the risk of SAD (adjusted OR: 0.78, p < 0.001). Even after balancing group differences through inverse probability treatment weighting, the results remained stable.

In elderly patients, long-term (current) aspirin use is negatively associated with the incidence of SAD and is also linked to improved clinical outcomes.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40520-025-03152-y.

Keywords: Older people, Long-term (current) use of aspirin, Sepsis, Delirium, NSAIDs, Neuropsychological tests
sections.introduction:
Sepsis is a life-threatening condition, characterized by organ dysfunction due to infection, with mortality rates exceeding 40%, imposing a substantial global healthcare burden [ 1 , 2 ]. Older adults are particularly susceptible to sepsis due to the impact of aging itself, coupled with multimorbidity, declining immunity, and functional limitations [ 3 ]. It is estimated that over 60% of sepsis cases occur in older adults, who also exhibit significantly higher mortality rates [ 4 , 5 ]. Even worse, with the continued trend of global aging, this proportion is expected to continue increasing [ 6 ]. Therefore, conducting prognostic research focused on elderly patients with sepsis is of importance.

Sepsis-associated delirium (SAD) is a common manifestation of brain dysfunction in older patients with sepsis. Its occurrence is closely associated with poor prognosis and serves as a key factor contributing to increased mortality, prolonged hospital stays, recurrent admissions, long-term cognitive impairment, and escalating healthcare expenditures [ 7 ]. The neurological deficits associated with SAD may persist for months or even longer, even after the sepsis episode subsides [ 8 ]. However, currently, there is no effective method to prevent or cure it. The most predominant strategy for managing delirium in the intensive care unit (ICU) is the avoidance of risk factors; however, this approach is inadequate, and the incidence of delirium remains alarmingly high [ 9 ]. Fortunately, in terms of intervention strategies, the ABCDEF bundle shows immense potential. A systematic review and meta-analysis revealed that the implementation of the ABCDEF bundle resulted in a 43% reduction in the incidence of delirium [ 10 ]. As part of the systematic approach within the ABCDEF bundle for the treatment and prevention of delirium, pharmacological interventions have shown promising potential [ 11 , 12 ]. A meta-analysis of high-quality randomized controlled trials demonstrated that the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) reduced the incidence of postoperative delirium by 46% [ 13 ]. This effect may be attributed to the anti-inflammatory properties of NSAIDs, as delirium is driven by neuroinflammation characterized by elevated levels of inflammatory mediators. NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, thereby suppressing prostaglandin synthesis and attenuating the inflammatory response [ 14 ].

As one of the most widely used NSAIDs globally, aspirin is renowned for its effectiveness and low cost, and is frequently prescribed for long-term use in the elderly. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) also recommends its use for the prevention of cardiovascular disease and colorectal cancer [ 15 , 16 ]. In patients with sepsis, anti-inflammatory effects of aspirin have also shown beneficial effects on inflammation-related activation pathways, and a history of its use—both prior to and following sepsis diagnosis—has been linked to improved survival rate [ 17 – 21 ].

However, evidence regarding its association with the development of delirium in sepsis patients remains limited. Given the inflammatory characteristics of sepsis and delirium, as well as the anti-inflammatory effects of aspirin, this study aims to investigate whether a history of long-term aspirin use is associated with the occurrence of SAD in elderly patients. Such findings may provide important evidence for the pharmacological prevention and treatment of delirium. This is particularly relevant in sepsis, where a heightened systemic inflammatory response significantly increases the risk of delirium [ 22 ]. Early administration of anti-inflammatory interventions may offer a more effective strategy for preventing SAD and improving patient prognosis. Therefore, we hypothesise that a history of long-term aspirin use reduces the incidence of SAD.
sections.methods:
All patient data in this study were sourced from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC IV) database (version 3.1), a free, publicly available, and high-quality database [ 23 ]. This latest version includes medical data from all ICU admissions at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in the United States from 2008 to 2022, including the COVID-19 pandemic period, providing deeper insights into patient behaviors and health trends. This database complies with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and all data have been de-identified, thereby exempting the need for patient consent or approval from an ethics committee. Xin Liang, one of the authors, underwent training and successfully passed the institutional assessment for access permissions (Record ID: 57086225).

This study was conducted in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines [ 24 ]. The elderly patients were all diagnosed with sepsis according to the Sepsis-3 criteria defined by the Third International Consensus on Sepsis and Septic Shock [ 25 ]. According to this definition, sepsis is identified by Sequential Organ Failure Score (SOFA) score of ≥ 2 along with confirmed or suspected infection. Suspected infection is defined as the administration of antibiotics within 3 days after culture collection or within 24 h prior [ 25 ]. According to this definition, we extracted 16,003 elderly sepsis patients (≥ 65 years) from the MIMIC database who were admitted to the ICU for the first time, and patients who developed delirium before the diagnosis of sepsis were also excluded. Eventually 9145 elderly septic patients were recruited into our study. The detailed screening process is shown in Fig. 1 .

Flow chart of study population. Note: By using IPTW to create a weighted sample to eliminate the observed systematic differences between treatment and control subjects. Abbreviations: MIMIC-IV, medical information mart for intensive care IV; ICU, intensive care units; IPTW, inverse probability treatment weighting

Patient treatment information was extracted using Structured Query Language (SQL) in Navicat Premium 15 software. All laboratory test data were measured after the patient was admitted to the ICU. We extract the first measurement after admission to the ICU, if there are multiple measurements of the same variables. The following data were ultimately extracted: (1) General information: age, gender, race, marital, insurance, History of smoking and alcohol consumption; (2) Vital signs: temperature, heart rate, resp rate mean arterial pressure (MBP), SPO 2 ; (3) Lab parameters: PO 2, PCO 2, PH, Platelet, red blood cell (RBC), white blood cell (WBC), Lactate, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, calcium, glucose, sodium, potassium; (4) First day’s urine output: urine output (5) Medical scores: Oxford acute severity of illness score (OASIS), Glasgow coma score (GCS), Braden score, SOFA, acute physiology score III (APS III), Charlson comorbidity index; (6) Comorbidities: malnutrition, diabetes, hypertension, myocardial infarct, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, dementia, chronic pulmonary disease, peptic ulcer disease, renal disease, malignant cancer; (7) Treatment and drugs: statin, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI), vasoactive, sedatives, renal replacement therapy (RRT), mechanical ventilation (MV). (8) outcomes: delirium, length of hospitalization, length of ICU, hospital expire flag, 30, and360 days mortality rate. The maximum percentage of missing values among the extracted variables does not exceed 20% (Supplemental Material Fig. 1 ), and multiple imputation is employed to handle the missing data (Supplemental Material Fig. 2 ).

The exposure variable in this study was long-term aspirin use, categorized as yes or no. The definition adheres to the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes of the 9th and 10th editions. Diagnoses were extracted from the MIMIC database using the following codes: ICD-9 code V58.66 and ICD-10 code Z79.82 (Long-term (current) aspirin use). This is defined as if the patient is receiving a medication for an extended period as a prophylactic measure (such as for the prevention of deep vein thrombosis) or as treatment of a chronic condition (such as arthritis) or a disease requiring a lengthy course of treatment (such as cancer).

The primary outcome of this study is delirium, while the secondary outcomes include hospital length of stay, ICU length of stay, in-hospital mortality, as well as 30-day and 360-day mortality in elderly patients with sepsis. Delirium was diagnosed by trained nurses using the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Additionally, key information on delirium was extracted from nursing text records in the “chartevents” table (itemid = 220001), which documented changes in patients’ mental status during hospitalization, including (1) delirium, (2) confusion, (3) agitation, and (4) altered mental status. Additionally, the MIMIC database provides post-discharge follow-up for each patient, with a maximum duration of 360 days. Using this follow-up data, the patient’s survival status at 30 and 360 days was determined by calculating the time from ICU admission to death.

First, a statistical description and comparison of intergroup differences were conducted. The normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test, which indicated that all variables deviated from the normality assumption. Consequently, continuous variables were expressed as medians with interquartile ranges, while categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. The Kruskal-Wallis test was employed for continuous variables, and Fisher’s exact test was used for categorical variables to compare differences between the exposed and non-exposed groups.

The association between long-term aspirin use and SAD was determined using multivariate logistic regression, and the odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. To this end, we constructed three models. Model 1 was unadjusted for covariates, Model 2 was adjusted for general information and vital signs, and Model 3 incorporated all covariates from Model 2 along with laboratory test results, first-day urine output, all scoring systems, comorbidities, and medications or therapeutic interventions, totaling 49 covariates. Given the large number of variables, to ensure model stability and avoid multicollinearity, we calculated the variance inflation factor (VIF) for each variable (Supplemental Material Table 1 ). A VIF < 5 was considered indicative of negligible multicollinearity [ 26 ]. To illustrate the impact of the long-term (current) aspirin use on the prognosis of elderly sepsis patients, we employed Kaplan-Meier survival curves to analyze survival at 30 and 360 days between the two groups. The log-rank test was used to assess differences in survival distributions between groups. Multiple linear regression and the Cox proportional hazards model were employed to identify associations with secondary outcomes.

To ensure the robustness of our results, we conducted two sensitivity analyses. First, we developed Model 4, in which inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to balance intergroup differences and simulate randomization. Logistic regression was then performed to calculate ORs and 95% CIs. Compared to propensity score matching (PSM), IPTW can retain most individuals in the analysis, thereby increasing the effective sample size [ 27 ]. The balance was deemed acceptable if the mean difference was less than 0.1 for each variable and overall [ 28 ]. This eliminated inter-group differences, enhancing the comparability of the results. Second, given the challenges in accurately assessing delirium among patients with dementia and those with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score ≤ 8 (deep coma), we sequentially excluded these patients. This allowed for a more refined analysis of the relationship between long-term aspirin use and delirium.

Finally, we conducted a subgroup analysis to further examine the association between long-term aspirin use and delirium across the following subgroups: gender (male/female), race (white/other), smoking (yes/no), statin (yes/no), ACEI (yes/no), RRT (yes/no), and cerebrovascular disease (yes/no).

All analyses were completed using R version 4.4.3( http://www.R-project.org , R Foundation). A two-sided p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant in the study.
sections.results:
A total of 9145 elderly (≥ 65 years) sepsis patients were included in the study. Table 1 presents the baseline characteristics before IPTW adjustment. Among these patients, males comprised 56.1% (5128/9145); and the incidence of SAD was 44.9% (4107/9145). In the study cohort, the incidence of SAD in patients with long-term (current) aspirin use was 31.9% (244/765), which was significantly lower than the 46.1% (3863/8380) in patients without long-term aspirin (current) use ( p < 0.001). Additionally, compared to the control group, patients with long-term (current) aspirin use exhibited lower in-hospital mortality (8.2% vs. 19.6%). Figure 2 illustrates the survival differences between the two groups at 30 and 360 days, while the control group exhibited longer hospital and ICU stays. These differences were statistically significant ( p < 0.05).

Table 2 displays the impact of long-term (current) aspirin use on delirium in elderly septic patients. The fully adjusted Model 3, shows that long-term (current) aspirin use is a protective factor against delirium in sepsis patients (adjusted OR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.65–0.94 p = 0.007). Even in the IPTW-adjusted Model 4, although the association was attenuated, our findings remained robust (after IPTW OR: 0.84, 95% CI: 0.79–0.89, p < 0.001). Elderly septic patients on long-term (current) aspirin use had a 16% lower risk of delirium compared to controls.

Table 3 presents the association between long-term (current) aspirin use and the risk of adverse outcomes in elderly sepsis patients. Specifically, the Cox proportional hazards model indicated that long-term (current) aspirin use was a protective factor against 360-day mortality in elderly sepsis patients. Multivariable logistic regression revealed a negative association between long-term (current) aspirin use and in-hospital mortality, while multiple linear regression showed that patients in the aspirin use group had shorter hospital stays and ICU durations.

To rule out other manifestations of brain dysfunction, we performed sensitivity analyses, examining the results after excluding patients with dementia and those in deep coma (GCS ≤ 8) separately (Supplemental Material Tables 3 and 4 ). In the cohort excluding dementia patients, the fully adjusted model showed a significant association (OR: 0.76, 95% CI: 0.63–0.92, p = 0.005), while the IPTW model further confirmed this relationship (OR: 0.81, 95% CI: 0.76–0.86, p < 0.001). Among non-comatose patients, although the fully adjusted model did not indicate a significant association, the IPTW model, after adjusting for confounders, demonstrated a robust result (OR: 0.83, 95% CI: 0.78–0.89, p < 0.001).

Finally, we conducted a subgroup analysis, to explore the relationship between long-term (current) aspirin use and the occurrence of SAD in elderly septic patients across different subgroups. Except for race, the interaction p -values for gender, smoking, statin, ACEI, RRT and cerebrovascular disease were all greater than 0.05. This indicates that the effect of long-term (current) aspirin use on delirium in elderly septic patients was consistent across these different subgroups. Although the interaction p -value for race was less than 0.05, long-term (current) aspirin use remained consistently associated with a reduced risk of delirium in both the White subgroup and the non-White subgroup of elderly septic patients. See Fig. 4 for details.

sections.discussion:
This large retrospective cohort study revealed a significant negative association between long-term (current) aspirin use and the incidence of SAD in elderly patients with sepsis. Their risk of delirium was potentially reduced by 16% compared to those without a history of aspirin use. In non-dementia patients and those without deep coma (GCS > 8), long-term (current) aspirin use remains negatively associated with the development of SAD. Subgroup analysis also demonstrated the stability of the results. We included seven subgroups: gender (male/female), race (white/other), smoking (yes/no), statin (yes/no), ACEI (yes/no), RRT (yes/no), and cerebrovascular disease (yes/no). These subgroups indicated that a history of long-term (current) aspirin use had beneficial effects on the incidence of SAD across different subgroups. Our study also found an interesting result: compared to White patients, elderly individuals of other racial backgrounds may derive greater benefits.

A history of NSAIDs use tends to reduce the risk of delirium [ 29 ]. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have reported that NSAIDs use can reduce postoperative delirium in elderly patients undergoing knee or hip replacement surgery [ 30 , 31 ]. Another large retrospective cohort study yielded similar results: NSAIDs were associated with a reduced risk of postoperative delirium following hip and knee replacement surgeries [ 32 ]. The anti-inflammatory properties of NSAIDs may be one of the reasons to prevent delirium. Aspirin exerts its anti-inflammatory effects as a prostaglandin inhibitor by irreversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX)-2 enzymes [ 33 , 34 ]. Peng and Zhao’s animal study found that the use of selective COX-2 nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs significantly reduced IL-1β, IL-6and TNF-α expression, as well as prostaglandin E levels [ 35 , 36 ]. These factors are all associated with the onset and progression of inflammation and are actively expressed in patients with delirium [ 37 ]. Moreover, Huang et al. demonstrated in a study on mice that perioperative use of ibuprofen can improve cognitive abilities, reduce systemic inflammation, and decrease glial activation [ 38 ]. In a clinical setting, preoperative administration of corticosteroids and ibuprofen can also improve postoperative cognitive function by modulating the inflammatory response [ 39 , 40 ]. Based on this, long-term use of anti-inflammatory drugs has become a potential treatment to reduce the risk of cognitive disorders such as dementia [ 41 , 42 ].

For patients with sepsis, the initial stage is often characterized by a heightened inflammatory response. Peripheral inflammatory stimuli alter the function and molecular composition of the blood-brain barrier, facilitating the passage of inflammatory mediators into the brain and triggering neuroinflammation, which in turn increases the susceptibility to delirium in septic patients [ 43 , 44 ]. The anti-inflammatory effects of aspirin may inhibit the development of neuroinflammation, thereby interrupting this pathological process. In addition, the analgesic properties of aspirin should not be overlooked. Its prolonged anti-inflammatory action may reduce pain sensitivity over time, potentially contributing to a lower incidence of delirium. Of course, this association between pain and SAD requires further validation through well-designed clinical studies.

Subgroup analyses revealed a significant interaction between race and long-term (current) aspirin use, suggesting that the protective effect may be more pronounced in non-White populations. In the United States, compared to White individuals, Black and Hispanic populations are more prone to poorer blood pressure control, dementia, and vascular cognitive impairment, with Black individuals facing a 2- to 4-fold higher risk of ischemic stroke than White individuals [ 45 , 46 ]. Therefore, non-White populations may experience greater benefits from aspirin use. Moreover, the MIMIC database is predominantly composed of White patients, making long-term (current) aspirin use more likely among them compared to other racial groups, as reflected in our baseline characteristics. However, overall, regardless of race, long-term (current) aspirin use demonstrates a beneficial effect on SAD.

In our study, elderly sepsis patients with long-term (current) aspirin use exhibited better overall outcomes, except for the 30-day mortality rate. One study found that, regardless of the timing of aspirin administration, it was associated with improved short- and long-term outcomes for septic patients [ 47 ]. Coincidentally, Chen et al. [ 19 ]conducted a rigorous investigation into the relationship between aspirin use and outcomes in patients with sepsis-related acute kidney injury, finding that the aspirin group exhibited a lower 90-day mortality risk. Additionally, there was no significant association between aspirin use and an increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. Aspirin likely provides effective resistance against the systemic immune-inflammatory response in septic patients, thereby improving prognosis. A study involving 52,982 sepsis patients found that those who took aspirin in the 90 days prior to sepsis onset had a lower 90-day mortality rate [ 20 ]. Several plausible mechanisms have been proposed regarding the association between the two. On one hand, aspirin can downregulate arachidonic acid and subsequent platelet aggregation by inhibiting COX-1. Since platelets play a role in the activation, amplification, and regulation of inflammation, inhibiting platelets may suppress severe systemic inflammatory responses [ 17 ]. On the other hand, aspirin directly inhibits the inflammatory response in sepsis by inhibiting the COX-2 and NF-κB pathways [ 17 ]. Additionally, in vitro experiments have shown that aspirin exhibits antibacterial properties. Administering aspirin before antibiotic treatment can inhibit the growth rate of Staphylococcus aureus vegetation in rats [ 48 ].

Currently, numerous studies have explored the relationship between aspirin and mortality rates in septic patients. However, we may be among the first to study this issue—delirium. SAD is a significant risk factor for the prognosis of elderly sepsis patients, and proactive prevention and treatment can help reduce unnecessary healthcare costs. The inflammatory properties of sepsis and delirium have the potential to make aspirin stand out - for preventing SAD. As a low-cost and effective anti-inflammatory medication, it is frequently prescribed by doctors to elderly patients, and increasing evidence suggests that aspirin may be a potential treatment and preventive drug for sepsis and delirium. Future foundational research is needed to explore the occurrence of these mechanisms. Aspirin is likely to be a simple, efficient, and cost-efficient way to prevent delirium, and it is also linked to improvements in other clinical outcomes among elderly patients with sepsis.

Although this study relies on a large sample from the database, adjusts for 49 covariates to enhance statistical precision and reduce result uncertainty, and employs two sensitivity analyses to validate the robustness of the relationship between long-term (current) aspirin use and the occurrence of SAD in elderly sepsis patients, several limitations still exist in this study. First, it is a retrospective study and cannot directly provide causal evidence. Second, due to inherent limitations of the database, we could not obtain specific information on the duration and dosage of long-term aspirin use, preventing further detailed analysis of dosage and duration. Studies have shown that high-dose aspirin (325 mg/day) is nearly equivalent to low-dose aspirin (75 mg/day) in preventing cardiovascular diseases, while long-term use (over one year) may offer greater benefits than short-term use (within one year) [ 49 ]. However, whether low-dose aspirin is safer and more effective than high-dose aspirin in preventing delirium remains unclear, and the impact of long-term use (several years) compared to short-term use (weeks or months) on delirium incidence warrants further investigation. Third, although we adjusted for 49 covariates to the best of our ability, the retrospective study design may still result in the omission of other important variables. Finally, reliance on nursing records and ICD coding to identify delirium and long-term aspirin use may lead to underreporting. More multi-centre, prospective approaches are needed in the future to further demonstrate their relationship.
sections.conclusion: Based on this large population-based retrospective cohort study, we investigated the association between long-term (current) aspirin use and the incidence of SAD in elderly patients. The results revealed a negative correlation between long-term (current) aspirin use and the occurrence of SAD and is also associated with improved clinical outcomes. The anti-inflammatory properties of aspirin, a medication frequently prescribed to the elderly, have demonstrated greater benefits in patients with sepsis and may represent a promising option for the prevention or treatment of SAD. In the future, further research is needed to solidify our findings.
